title: NURS 1021 Unit 1 Case Study 7

question.stem: The nurse reviews the Health History and the Physical Assessment. Highlight the findings that are consistent with vitamin B12 deficiency.
question.explanation:
Anemia: tiredness and pallor; the slight yellow tinge comes from pallor combined with mild jaundice, because abnormal red cell precursors are destroyed in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) and release bilirubin.

Glossitis: a red, smooth, burning tongue, because rapidly dividing cells of the tongue also need B12 to make DNA.

Neurologic findings (unique to B12 deficiency): B12 is needed to maintain myelin. Damage to the dorsal columns of the spinal cord and peripheral nerves causes numbness and tingling in a stocking distribution, loss of vibration and position sense, a positive Romberg test, and an unsteady gait that is worse in the dark, when the client cannot use vision to make up for lost position sense; hence falls at night. Cognitive and mood changes (forgetfulness, irritability, depression) also occur. These can appear before the anemia and become permanent if treatment is delayed.

Not consistent: pain and temperature sensation are usually spared in B12 deficiency. A diet with meat, eggs and dairy supplies B12, so the cause is poor absorption, not intake. No black or bloody stools makes blood loss unlikely.

leftContent.intro: The nurse on a medical unit is caring for a 61-year-old female client admitted for investigation of anemia after two falls at home.

question.stem: The nurse explains the differences between the two vitamin deficiencies. For each finding, click to specify whether it occurs in vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, or both.

rows.text: MCV above 100 fL with hypersegmented neutrophils
Loss of vibration and position sense with an unsteady gait
Common in alcohol use disorder and in pregnancy without supplements
Caused by a lack of intrinsic factor

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 1730 and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Both: B12 and folate are both needed to make DNA. Without either, cells keep growing (RNA and protein synthesis continue) but divide poorly, so red cells are large (megaloblastic, MCV above 100 fL) and neutrophils have extra nuclear lobes. Folate needs B12 to be recycled, and both are needed to convert homocysteine to methionine, so homocysteine rises in both.

Vitamin B12 only: B12 is also needed to convert methylmalonyl-CoA, so methylmalonic acid rises only in B12 deficiency; the client's MMA of 1.9 µmol/L with a B12 of 98 pmol/L and normal folate confirm B12 deficiency. Neurologic damage occurs only in B12 deficiency. Intrinsic factor, made by gastric parietal cells, is needed to absorb B12 in the terminal ileum.

Folate only: folate stores last only months, so deficiency develops with poor intake (alcohol use disorder), increased need (pregnancy) or drugs such as methotrexate and phenytoin.

Folic acid alone: it could improve the blood count while the nerve damage progresses, so the nurse advises the client not to take it unless prescribed.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The client's red cells are large because [[drop0]]. The deficiency is mainly caused by [[drop1]]. The nurse's priority is [[drop2]].

options.text: too little iron is available to make hemoglobin
the spleen releases young red cells early
the cells swell from too much water inside them
DNA synthesis is impaired, so precursor cells grow but divide too few times
blood loss from the stomach
too little folate in the diet
too little vitamin B12 in the diet
antibodies that block intrinsic factor (pernicious anemia)
teaching the client how to give injections
preventing falls caused by loss of position sense
relieving the burning tongue
preventing infection from a low white cell count

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 0900 and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Large cells: without B12, DNA synthesis is impaired while RNA and protein synthesis continue, so precursors grow large but divide fewer times; many die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis), raising LDH and bilirubin. Iron deficiency makes cells small.

Cause: in pernicious anemia, autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells, and antibodies block intrinsic factor, so B12 cannot be absorbed in the ileum. It is often associated with other autoimmune diseases such as autoimmune thyroid disease. Metformin and reduced stomach acid (omeprazole) add to poor absorption. The client's diet contains B12, and folate is normal.

Priority: the client has already fallen twice, has lost position sense and gets up alone at night: injury from falls is the most immediate risk. The white cell count is only mildly low; glossitis and teaching follow.

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in the client's plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Teach the client that eating more meat and dairy will correct the deficiency
Inspect the client's feet daily for injuries the client may not feel
Keep the client on bed rest until the hemoglobin is normal
Offer soft, bland foods and mouth care with a soft toothbrush
Give the cyanocobalamin injections as prescribed
Give folic acid tablets instead of injections, since they are easier to take
Keep the bed low, the call bell in reach and a night light on, and assist the client when walking

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 1000 and the Orders.
question.explanation:
Include: in pernicious anemia the oral B12 in food cannot be absorbed, so B12 is given by injection (Option 5). Fall precautions protect the client while position sense is lost (Option 7). Loss of sensation in the feet means injuries can go unnoticed (Option 2). Glossitis makes spicy, hot and acidic foods painful (Option 4).

Do not include: folic acid can correct the anemia but not the nerve damage, which can progress (Option 6). Without intrinsic factor, dietary B12 is not absorbed (Option 1). Bed rest increases weakness and deconditioning; the client walks with assistance and physiotherapy (Option 3).

leftContent.intro: The nurse on a medical unit is caring for a 61-year-old female client admitted for investigation of anemia after two falls at home.

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated.

rows.text: Contact the internist to clarify the message before changing the treatment
Give folic acid 5 mg PO daily and hold the cyanocobalamin
Give today's cyanocobalamin dose into the deltoid muscle
Give the cyanocobalamin as an IV push to avoid an injection
Request a bone marrow biopsy to confirm the diagnosis
Walk with the client using a gait belt to the bathroom

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 1100.
question.explanation:
Contraindicated: giving folate alone to a client with B12 deficiency can improve the blood count while the neurologic damage continues, and holding B12 delays treatment that should start at once; gastroscopy does not require it to be held. Cyanocobalamin is given IM (or deep subcutaneously); given IV, most of it is lost in the urine before it can be used.

Indicated: an order that conflicts with the diagnosis and the existing plan is clarified with the prescriber before acting. The prescribed IM dose is given. A gait belt and assistance protect the client from falls.

Non-Essential: low B12, high methylmalonic acid and positive intrinsic factor antibodies already confirm the diagnosis; a bone marrow biopsy is not needed.

leftContent.intro: The nurse on a medical unit is caring for a 61-year-old female client admitted for investigation of anemia after two falls at home.

question.stem: Which statements by the client indicate an understanding of the teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: “I will need B12 injections every month for the rest of my life.”
“I'll tell my doctor if the tingling gets worse or my balance changes.”
“Now that my blood count is normal, I can stop the injections.”
“I'll check my feet every day, because I may not feel a cut or blister.”
“Eating liver once a week will keep my B12 up.”
“I can switch to my neighbour's folic acid tablets instead of the injections.”
“The numbness in my feet may take months to improve and might not go away completely.”

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 1200 and Week 6 1000, the Vital Signs, and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Response: reticulocytes rose sharply by day 7 (14 to 198 × 10⁹/L), the expected first sign of response, and by week 6 hemoglobin, MCV, white cells and platelets have returned to normal. Neurologic recovery is slower.

Understood: the cause, loss of intrinsic factor, is permanent, so B12 is given for life (Option 1). Nerve recovery takes months and may be incomplete, especially when symptoms were present for a long time (Option 7). Reduced sensation means daily foot checks (Option 4). Worsening neurologic symptoms suggest inadequate treatment (Option 2).

Needs more teaching: stopping injections leads to relapse (Option 3). Folic acid does not treat B12 deficiency and can hide it while nerve damage progresses (Option 6). Dietary B12 cannot be absorbed without intrinsic factor (Option 5).

description: 61-year-old female with pernicious anemia (plus metformin and omeprazole) presenting with falls, paresthesias and glossitis: megaloblastic anemia, vitamin B12 versus folate deficiency (methylmalonic acid, homocysteine), IM cyanocobalamin and why folate alone is unsafe.

authorReview.note: New case written by Claude on 25 Nov 2026 (NURS 1021 Unit 1, batch 2); checked against Merck Manual Professional (Vitamin B12 Deficiency, Jun 2026; Folate Deficiency, Nov 2026; Megaloblastic Macrocytic Anemias, Mar 2025). Please review: methylmalonic acid (< 0.40 µmol/L) and homocysteine (5–15 µmol/L) reference ranges (not in the MCC list); the cyanocobalamin schedule (daily × 7, weekly × 4, then monthly; Merck gives 1 mg IM 1–4 times a week, then monthly); outpatient gastroscopy at diagnosis of pernicious anemia.
